title: FAST '26 - Sharpen the Spec, Cut the Code: A Case for Generative File System with SYSSPEC
transcriptText:
Hello everyone. I'm Qingyuan from
Shanghai Jiao Tong University. I'm glad
to present our work about a case for the
generative file system paradigm with
C-spec.
A file system is a cornerstone of
operating systems, bridging the gaps
between application and storage devices.
It keeps evolving since hardware and
applications
Uh, sorry.
Um, it keeps evolving since hardware and
applications are continuously updating.
For instance, the emergence of flash and
LLMs led to the development of F2FS and
the Firefly file system respectively.
Beyond the burst of new systems, mature
file systems like EXT4 have also
continuously integrated new features
over the past 20 years.
So, to um,
to achieve the aforementioned
development and evolution of the file
system, the community has invested
tremendous effort. For instance, our
statistics show that Linux has seen more
than um, 3,000 EXT4 related commits over
the past 20 years. These efforts involve
extensive coding to implement new
features, which account for only 5% of
the commits, but represent 18 18% of the
total lines of code.
Um, the effort also includes the
long-tail maintenance and bug fixing.
These two types of commits take more
than 80% of total commits.
Um, ti- times are changing. Today, the
coding capabilities of LLMs are
advancing rapidly.
Data from OpenRouter shows that tokens
consumed by programming tasks searched
in the past 6 months accounting for more
than half of the total token usage. This
leads to a natural question. Why not use
LLMs to reduce the manual effort
required for file system development and
evolution?
To this end, we propose a paradigm of
generative file system.
Our vision is for programmers to focus
focus solely on system design,
eliminating the need for manual coding.
Specifically, developers will only need
to specify the file system's behavior
through high-level specifications. The
coding responsibility is then shifted to
LLMs, which translate these
specifications into a concrete
implementation.
This paradigm is not limited to
construct a file system from scratch. It
also enables file system evolution
through specification updates. After
updating the specifications, the
system's implementation is automatically
refreshed by the LLM.
Essentially, the entire evolution
process also becomes code-free. In a
word, we believe this paradigm could
significantly boost productivity in both
the development and evolution of file
systems.
To realize the paradigm, we need
systematic methodology that defines how
to execute each core step. These steps
include
specifying the file system logic,
updating those specifications, and
generating code from them.
Unfortunately, it's not easy to
accomplish these tasks, achieving the
paradigm of generative file system and
realize robust code generation.
Specifically, we identify at least four
challenges.
The first challenge is the semantic
gaps. That is, there's lack of
systematic methodology for specifying
the functionality and the behavior of
programs. Currently, people simply use
arbitrary or random natural language to
tell LLMs what code to generate.
However, the semantic information in
these prompts may be insufficient or for
the LLM to generate the code they want.
Um the behavior of programs with
concurrency
or multi-threading is even more complex
and difficult to specify. For example,
if you ask the LLM to generate a file
system with requirements like no
dependency errors or avoid race
conditions with locking, the LLM may
fail to understand your intent and
instead generate misbehaved or buggy
code. For complex systems like a file
system, even the slightest deviation in
behavior can cause the entire system to
crash. This is simply unacceptable.
The second challenge arises from the
structural complexity of file system
modules. Given the large number of
modules and their intricate
dependencies, attempting to generate the
entire file system
the entire file system in a single pass
could easily exceed context limits. Our
experiments shows that generating just
200 lines of C code requires
approximately 30,000 tokens with
DeepSeek-R1. Conversely, if we try to
build the complete file system through
multiple generations, the lack of shared
context between these steps makes it
highly prone to dependency errors or the
interface mismatches.
The third challenge is that we must
ensure backward compatibility when
involving the file system.
If we update the modules, for example,
update the module C here,
we need to ensure that the functionality
of other dependent modules remains
correct, preventing this modification
from creating a cascading effect.
Finally, the LLM's capability is
unreliable. It could generate unstable
outputs even with the same input and
could suffer from hallucinations. For
example, when generating the code like
this, the LLM could occasionally forget
to lock root LLM because of the
hallucinated safe state.
So, to address the challenges,
we propose SysFS
a framework of generative file system.
First, the design of SysFS
specification specifies the file system
and addresses the challenge of lacking
systematic methodology for specifying
programs and the challenge of
complicated composition.
Second, the design of SysFS patch is
responsible to update the
specifications, addressing the challenge
of backward compatibility upon file
system evolution.
Third, the design of SysFS tool chain
generates the code from specifications,
addressing the challenge of unstable LLM
capabilities.
Now, let me introduce these designs one
by one.
First is the design of SysFS
specification. The key insight of this
design stems from our observation that
generative file systems and formal
verification share strong similarities.
Specifically, the generative file system
paradigm uses the specification to
generate the implementation with the
with the specification. In contrast, the
formal verification verifies the
existence implementation with formal
specification, and the formal
specification can be highly precise.
So, in conclusion, the generative file
system paradigm uses the SysFS uses the
specification to generate rather than
verify the file system implementation.
Therefore, we could borrow methodology
from formal specifications to address
the challenges of specifying the file
system, and we exactly did that. Our
design of SysFS heavily draws
inspiration from formal verification.
First, um we continue to use the module
as the basic unit of specification and
code generation. A module is a
collection of one or more functions, and
a specification-based file system
similarly consists of multiple
specification modules.
For each module, the C spec
specification is structured with three
components: the functionality,
concurrency, and modular specifications.
Functionality specification defines the
functional functional logic of each
module. Concurrency specification
specify concurrent behavior and
interactions. And the modularity
specification describes inter-module
composition and dependencies. Together,
they address the first two challenges.
First, the functionality specification
borrows the whole logic from formal
verification. Basically, it has a whole
logic style semantics, includes
pre-condition, post-condition, and
invariants. Pre-condition specifies the
required state before execution. And
post-condition describes the guaranteed
state upon completion.
The invariant describes properties that
must hold true across state transitions.
To make the specification more
accessible to programmers, we allow the
use of natural language to describe
mathematical relations in whole logic.
Of course, this introduces a trade-off
increasing ambiguity. We believe this
trade-off can be worthwhile since our
evaluation demonstrates that LLMs can
tolerate some ambiguities to some extent
and generate the code correctly.
In addition, functionality
specifications may include optional
supplementary semantic information such
as intent or system algorithm. Details
can be found in the paper.
The functionality specification focuses
solely on the sequential logic of the
program. As a complement to that, the
concurrency specification focuses on the
concurrent execution behavior. Using
whole style specifications, it specifies
the locking state for each step within
the module, such as for each function
call. Moreover,
separating sequential and concurrent
logic facilitates two-stage generation
process. Generates the sequential logic
first, then complement logic and locking
logics.
In our early experiment, this approach
has occasionally improved the generation
accuracy.
Then, the modularity specification is
responsible to describe the interface
level dependencies between modules. To
avoid exceeding the context window, each
module is typically less than 500 lines
of code. The modularity specification
borrows rely and guarantee phases from
formal verification. Since rely and
guarantee is used to specify a module's
assumption about other components.
Specifically, rely is external
dependencies required by the
implementation of this module. In turn,
guarantee describes behaviors
implemented and exposed by this module.
The rely and guarantee inherently
describes the dependency relationships
between modules. We hope the
specification based file system is
constructed with DAG structured
dependencies.
In addition to construct a file system
from scratch with specifications, our
design of SpecPatch is responsible for
guiding the evolution of file system,
addressing the challenge of backward
compatibility.
The DAG structure of specifications is
natural for evolution. Meanwhile, we
also organize the modified or new
specifications into the DAG structure,
forming a DAG structured specification
patch. Generally speaking, the DAG
structured SpecPatch has two types of
node.
The non-root nodes implement and expose
new guarantees. Then, the entire patch
must contain at least one root node to
be considered complete. The root node
could rely on the new guarantees, but
most importantly, its own guarantees do
not change. Therefore, the root node can
serve as the commit point to
merge the SpecPatch DAG into the
original specification stack.
The patch merging process is easy.
We replace the specification of the old
root node with a new one.
The whole patch is thus merged into
original specifications automatically
and avoid cascading dependency issues.
Finally, um we will want to introduce
the C spec tool chain. The C spec tool
chain is responsible to generate the
implementation from specifications.
The generation process is a feedback
loop with multiple agents.
First, with the specification of a
module, the spec compiler is responsible
to generate a draft version of
implementation. Subsequently, spec
validator validates the generated code.
The verification can be conducted using
prepared unit tests or simply by letting
the LLM review the code and determine
whether it aligns with the
specification.
If the validation fails, the validator
feeds the failure information back to
spec compiler, which uh regenerates the
code based on the feedbacks.
The feedback loop effectively mitigates
hallucinations and ensure that the
generated code adheres closely to the
specification. In our experiment, about
30% of modules retry at least once
generating misbehaved the code um in the
first pass of generation.
Um we also prepare an agent called spec
assistant assisting um developers in
generating spec specifications. Details
can be found in the paper.
Um with with C spec, we construct spec
FS as a case study. Spec FS is a
concurrent file system completely
implemented with specifications without
any manual coding.
The implementation is based on AtomFS
from SOSP '19, a formally verified
concurrent file system.
We further add 10 extra features from
EXT4 to SpecFS, including the feature of
extended data allocation and so on. With
all the integrated features, SpecFS has
about 4,000 lines of code. The these
lines of code could rank 42 out of the
82 file systems from Linux 6 kernel.
We have evaluated the functional
correctness of SpecFS.
A module is considered correct if it
passes all functional tests for AtomFS
and is deemed logically equivalent to
AtomFS through manual inspection.
The result is that with most LLMs, the
45 modules and 70 modules for features
are 100% correct. It means that it has
the same level of correctness as
human-written AtomFS. This result is
also reproducible. We also find that
with small modules like Queen 3 32
billion, some modules always fail
even with multi turns of feedback loops.
The errors mainly result from concurrent
modules fail to handle the complicated
concurrent logic.
Generated file system also improves the
productivity. Compared with C
implementation, specification has
evidently less lines of code. And
moreover, we invited four graduate
students to implement two features of
SpecFS, recorded the time they spent
implementing the implementing the
corresponding functionality and found
that their productivity productivity was
improved with C-spec compared with the
way of manual coding. This aligns with
our experience. Writing specifications
better matches human practice, does not
require attending to every detail, and
can therefore be completed more quickly
than writing code.
In conclusion, we propose the paradigm
of generated file system and design a
framework, Cspec, to realize that
paradigm. With Cspec, we implement um
SpecFS as a case study, generate the
whole SpecFS from scratch, and further
implement 10 features from EXT4 for it.
We finally validated the feasibility of
the paradigm. SpecFS achieves equivalent
level of correctness compared with
human-written code. The productivity is
also improved.
Here's the main page of our project. In
addition to our paper, it includes the
code we submitted for artifact
evaluation and a data set containing the
statistics on EXT4 patches. Thank you
very much.
